newsitem.title: USA: Republican says Clinton Medicare plan not enough.
newsitem.headline: Republican says Clinton Medicare plan not enough.

text.p: A key House Republican said Friday President Clinton's proposal for $138 billion in Medicare cuts needed major revisions, adding Republicans would push for malpractice reform and possible expansion of tax-free medical savings accounts.

California Republican Rep. Bill Thomas, chairman of the House Ways and Means subcommittee that oversees Medicare, made it clear Republicans wanted major revisions in Clinton's plan for six-year Medicare cuts. He said the $46 billion in managed care cuts were too big and called a plan to transfer some home health costs a "gimmick."
"They aren't strong on reform, they're big on reduction," Thomas told the National Academy of Social Insurance.
Thomas said Republicans would press ahead with a medical malpractice reform bill, which could either be brought to a vote as part of a Medicare package or free-standing bill.
"That will be a provision that we will offer ... we will offer it until we are successful," Thomas said.
An unsuccessful Medicare plan crafted by House Republicans during the last Congress would have give senior citizens the option of tax-free medical savings accounts to cover health insurance needs.
Thomas said Republicans still wanted to look at the accounts, possibly as a Medicare option. Clinton did not support the plan last time around.

Republicans, who were attacked by Democrats in the November elections, who said their propoal for $270 billion in Medicare cuts would have savaged the program. Thomas said Republicans had learned from that experience and did not plan to offer major cuts beyond those contained in Clinton's budget.

For example, Clinton has said that he is not adverse to the idea of requiring well-off senior citizens to pay more for Medicare Part B doctors' premiums. Thomas said Republians have supported such a proposal in the past, but would not offer it unless Clinton specifically recommended it first.
He criticized the White House for recommending $46 billion in reductions to managed care plans over six years.
He also slammed White House proposals to shift about $60 billion in Medicare's fast growing home health program from the Part A trust fund, which faces bankruptcy, to Part B.
